source: Patel and Groen (1986) Knowledge based solution strategies in medical reasoning (Cognitive Science 10:91-116), abstract via Crossref
finding: Founding study. Seven cardiologists diagnosed one case of acute bacterial endocarditis and explained its pathophysiology. Physicians with accurate diagnoses showed pure forward reasoning through causal rules. Those with inaccurate diagnoses mixed forward and backward reasoning, starting from a high-level hypothesis.
numbers: N = 7 cardiologists, 1 case. Abstract gives no per-group counts. Crossref lists 427 citations.
quote: explanations of physicians making an accurate diagnosis can be accounted for in terms of a model consisting of pure forward reasoning
limits: Only the abstract was read (full text blocked). One case, seven people, hand-coded propositional analysis. The link is accuracy-to-direction, not expertise-to-direction.
agent_relevance: Confirms the founding evidence is tiny. Forward-only went with accuracy in this one case; do not treat it as a law for the agent.

source: Groen and Patel (1985) Medical problem-solving: some questionable assumptions (Medical Education 19:95-100), abstract via Crossref
finding: Argues that the claim 'expert doctors use hypothetico-deductive reasoning' was never shown empirically. Expert-novice work in cognitive psychology suggests hypothetico-deductive use is a feature of novices. Experts use strong, knowledge-dependent methods.
quote: the use of the hypothetico-deductive method is a characteristic of novices rather than experts
limits: Abstract only. Argument, not an experiment. Written one year before the 1986 data paper by the same authors.
agent_relevance: Shows the forward-expert idea began as a critique of the textbook model, not as a replicated effect.

source: Review (2023) Cognitive perspectives on maintaining physicians' medical expertise II (PMC10366061)
finding: A recent review states that changes in hypothetico-deductive problem solving do not appear to explain the novice-to-expert transition, citing Boshuizen and Schmidt 1992, Elstein and Schwarz 2002, Groen and Patel 1985, Neufeld 1981 and Norman 2005. It adds that experts still use hypothetico-deductive analysis when they slow down.
quote: changes in hypothetico-deductive problem solving do not appear to explain the transition from novices to experts
limits: Secondary source; the cited primary papers were not opened. It does not report a direct failed replication of the 1986 result.
agent_relevance: Supports reading direction as a switchable strategy used by everyone, not an expertise marker. Matches claim K02.

source: Schmidt and Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation (Medical Education 41:1133-1139), abstract via Crossref
finding: Review of 30 years of work. Most studies fit the view that biomedical knowledge becomes encapsulated into illness scripts with experience. Debate remains about the role of biomedical knowledge in case processing.
numbers: Review; no figures in the abstract.
quote: there is still debate concerning the role of biomedical knowledge in clinical case processing
limits: Abstract only. This is the Rikers/Schmidt line that explains expertise by knowledge structure rather than by reasoning direction. The 1997 Rikers paper itself was not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: expertise is stored scripts, not a direction. For the agent this means supply the right knowledge, not a direction rule.

source: Lopez et al. (2026) Clinician input steers AI toward accurate and harmful recommendations (arXiv 2603.14158)
finding: 61 NEJM case records, 21 reasoning variants of 8 models. A misleading clinician differential supplied up front lowered inclusion of the correct final diagnosis in 14 of 21 models after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. An expert differential raised it in all 21.
numbers: Adversarial context: mean -5.4 points (range +0.2 to -29.8); GPT-4o -29.8 (p<0.001); LLaMA-3.3-70B -17.2. Expert context: mean +20.4 points, all 21 significant. Adversarial context cut leading-diagnosis accuracy significantly in 13 models.
quote: adversarial clinician context caused significant diagnostic degradation in 14 models (mean -5.4 percentage points)
limits: Supplied content is a clinician's differential with rationale, not a bare candidate list. Expert gain partly reflects echoing. Text vignettes.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 8: a wrong supplied hypothesis set hurts LLMs, and the harm depends on the model. The agent should not accept a pre-supplied differential without a hypothesis-blind first pass.

source: Lopez et al. (2026) reasoning effort and adversarial vulnerability (arXiv 2603.14158)
finding: More inference-time reasoning reduced harm from misleading clinician input in GPT-5 and Qwen3. Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini-3-Pro families showed no meaningful change with reasoning amount. Pattern is model-specific, not universal.
numbers: GPT-5 LLM-alone accuracy 75.5% (no reasoning) to 82.5% (medium/high). Adversarial gap 10.4 points (no reasoning) to 1.7-4.4 (higher reasoning). Qwen3: non-thinking -11.7 (p<0.001), thinking -3.9 (p<0.001). Google variants all under 3 points loss.
limits: Reasoning amount, not instructed direction, was varied. No difficulty stratification reported in the part read. Dose-response only clear for GPT-5.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: model strength and thinking budget interact with a bias manipulation, as expertise did in Bass 2013. Direction instruction x difficulty is still untested.

finding: Prompt cues about the clinician's uncertainty or inexperience recovered the accuracy lost to adversarial context while keeping the expert-context gain, in GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash. Claude Sonnet 4.5 only partly recovered.
numbers: Baseline adversarial loss: GPT-5 10.4 points (75.5 to 65.1), Claude Sonnet 4.5 3.2 (70.5 to 67.3), Gemini 3 Flash 2.9 (76.6 to 73.7). With the uncertainty cue Claude reached 73.0%, still marginally below alone (p=0.045).
limits: Cue carries content about source reliability, not a generic 'be careful'. Three models only in this step.
agent_relevance: Content-bearing framing (how reliable is the supplied hypothesis) works where generic caution does not. Gives a concrete form for a hypothesis-source tag in the schema.

source: Chen, Huang, Wang, Zhu (2026) MedEinst, ACL 2026 long paper 1847, Table 1 re-read
finding: The paper contradicts itself on which models have the top baseline accuracy. Text (twice) says GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro have 54.30% and 53.58%. The Table 1 rows put 54.30 and 53.58 on Baichuan-M2-32B and Lingshu-32B, which have trap rates 66.10 and 54.20. The Table 1 text layout is otherwise shifted: Table A2 gives Qwen3-32B as 40.25 / 11.86 / 43.46.
numbers: Table 1 trap rates: Gemini-2.5-pro 60.90, GPT-5 51.87, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98, Baichuan-M2-32B 66.10, Lingshu-32B 54.20, Qwen3-14B 54.19, DeepSeek-R1 46.12, Kimi-k2 47.12. 5,383 counterfactual pairs, 49 pathologies, 8 departments.
quote: frontier models like GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro achieve the highest baseline accuracy (54.30% and 53.58%)
limits: Which model owns 54.30 cannot be settled from the paper. The robust claim is weaker: high-accuracy rows (Baichuan 54.30, Lingshu-32B 53.58) and frontier rows both show trap rates above 50%. Author-stated inverse scaling rests on a 49-pathology set.
agent_relevance: Closes the table question: trust trap rates, treat baseline-accuracy attribution as unresolved. The anchor effect on strong models stands but the 'higher accuracy, higher trap' rank claim is weak.

source: MedEinst ablation (Table 2) of ECR-Agent on Qwen3-32B
finding: Adding the dynamic causal graph module (forward evidence plus backward shadow-node penalty) raised base accuracy and cut trap rate. Adding experience memory raised it further. No ablation isolates the shadow-node penalty alone.
numbers: Qwen3-32B: base 40.25 / robust 11.86 / trap 43.46. + DCI: 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32. + DCI + CGME: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75. Shadow-node score S(d) = wm*Nmatch - wc*Nconf - ws*Nshadow.
limits: Single base model. DCI bundles forward retrieval, backward counterfactual and shadow penalty, so the shadow effect is not separable. Trap rate fell only 5.1 points from DCI, and 4.6 more from memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 second half stays open: no shadow-only test exists. The structured check helps accuracy more than it lowers trap rate.

source: MedEinst stress test with an explicit warning prompt (Table A2)
finding: Adding an explicit warning against misleading distractors to zero-shot CoT raised baseline accuracy but raised the trap rate. A generic caution made anchoring worse on trap cases.
numbers: Qwen3-32B: acc 40.25 to 52.60, robust acc 11.86 to 8.70, trap 43.46 to 60.50. Qwen3-235B: acc 40.51 to 53.30, robust 11.40 to 9.20, trap 43.32 to 58.00.
quote: the explicit warning exacerbates the bias
limits: Two Qwen models; the authors' account (warning strengthens the prior) is a hypothesis. Robust accuracy is low in all arms.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a generic 'beware of bias' line can backfire. Keep the schema's checks content-bearing (name the finding to look for).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf (arXiv 2407.07330), other base models
finding: The Dual-Inf gain over self-consistency CoT is not GPT-only. It held for GPT-4o, Llama3-70B and BioLlama3-70B, all p<0.001.
numbers: DDx accuracy difference over SC-CoT across the three non-GPT-4 bases: 0.059, 0.048, 0.049 (GPT-4: 0.533 v 0.472, +0.061, CI 0.055-0.062). Interpretation accuracy on Llama bases: more than 17% above SC-CoT. 570 notes, nine specialties, five runs.
limits: Reported as averages over five runs, so the CI is across runs, not across cases. No token or call count is matched. Dual-Inf uses more modules than SC-CoT.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 first half closed: gain survives open-weight models. Compute-matched comparison still missing.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf ablation and error analysis, re-read (arXiv 2407.07330)
finding: Full Dual-Inf beats every ablated variant on GPT-4. The error comparison (factual errors up, missing content down) is against SC-CoT on 100 notes where SC-CoT was wrong, not against its own ablations, so the backward module is not shown to cause the factual errors.
numbers: GPT-4 DDx accuracy of ablations: 0.443, 0.449, 0.453, 0.497 versus full 0.533 (table text garbled; paper text says FI-EM near 0.5 and Dual-Inf about 7% better). Errors per 100: missing content about 89 v 76; factual 8.2 v 17; low relevance 10.8 v 15.4 (SC-CoT v Dual-Inf).
limits: Variant-to-row mapping of Table 3 is uncertain. No cost, token or call accounting appears in the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5 second half stay open. Treat the backward check as a plausible gain with a possible factual-error cost until a matched-token test exists.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: A generic 'review your answer' prompt without external feedback did not help and often hurt. With oracle labels telling the model when it was wrong, accuracy rose strongly.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; GPT-4 HotpotQA 29.0 to 59.0 (100 questions).
limits: Math and QA, not diagnosis. Generic reflect prompt, not a findings-based check. Small HotpotQA sample.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: generic reflection is a poor design; matches Norman 2014 and Kaemmer 2021 in humans. Checks should bring external or content-specific evidence.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2309.03882)
finding: 20 LLMs on three benchmarks show a selection bias toward option IDs such as A. An explicit debiasing instruction and zero-shot CoT did not fix it on gpt-3.5-turbo. Permutation-based debiasing worked and boosted llama-30b by 15.2 points.
numbers: Reported: llama-30b after debiasing 68.2 v gpt-3.5-turbo 65.3 on one benchmark. Removing option IDs helped only partly. Tables garbled in extraction.
quote: the two prompting strategies cannot mitigate selection bias well
limits: Format bias, not reasoning direction. Not a medical study. Does not test option-first versus blind-first generation.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 background: options change model behaviour and a polite instruction does not remove it. Use blind-first generation, then compare to options.

source: Myrzakhan, Bsharat, Shen (2024) Open-LLM-Leaderboard: from multi-choice to open-style questions (arXiv 2406.07545)
finding: Converting filtered multiple-choice items to open-style questions lowers accuracy for every model tested. Part of the MCQ score is guessing and option effects.
numbers: Average open-style accuracy about 25% lower than MCQ across models; GPT-4o top at 70.15% overall. Open-style grading by gpt-4-0125-preview.
limits: Confounds guessing with option-induced backward reasoning. Not medical. LLM grader. Does not isolate option-first reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only indirectly informed. Benchmark MCQ scores overstate blind diagnosis; run the agent blind first when real use has no options.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Quantifying the reasoning abilities of LLMs on real-world clinical cases, MedR-Bench (arXiv 2503.04691)
finding: Five reasoning LLMs on 1,453 case-report cases. Diagnosis rises as more information is supplied. Reasoning text is factually reliable but often misses key steps. The paper does not code reasoning direction.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 diagnostic accuracy 71.79% (1-turn), 76.18% (free-turn), 89.76% (oracle). o3-mini 64.99% to 67.19% (1-turn to free-turn). All models above 80% in the oracle setting. Factuality above 90%; exam-recommendation recall 43.61% best (R1, 1-turn).
limits: Does not label traces forward or backward, so it does not answer gap 6. 656 rare-disease cases; LLM-based Reasoning Evaluator.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models are accurate when findings are complete and weak at asking for the right findings, which is the hypothesis-driven part. Supports a backward 'what to ask next' step. Gap 6 stays open.

source: Li et al. (2026) Green Shielding: LLM-assisted medical diagnosis case study (arXiv 2604.24700)
finding: Neutralising patient-style wording in the query made differentials shorter and more plausible but cut coverage of likely and safety-critical conditions. Physicians write narrower differentials than models.
numbers: Qualitative trade-off reported in the abstract; HCM-Dx benchmark; exact figures not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and a structure scan read. Not about direction.
agent_relevance: Narrowing the hypothesis set trades coverage for plausibility; keep a coverage check for dangerous diagnoses when the agent prunes.

source: Gap note (2026): searches for LLM studies of direction by difficulty, equal-token backward checks, reasoning-model trace labels, and failed replications of Patel and Groen
finding: No study was found for any of: equal-token backward check versus self-consistency; forward-first versus hypothesis-first prompts by difficulty; forward/backward labelling of reasoning-model traces; option-first versus blind-first in medicine; Patel 1990, Patel 1994 and Rikers 1997 numbers.
numbers: WebSearch budget exhausted after the first query. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search endpoints returned rate-limit or empty answers.
limits: Absence reflects tool limits, not proof that the studies do not exist.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 2, 6 and 9 as open and testable in our own harness.
